c79-m1.summary: The New York Times announced recently that their Dec. 31 print issue would be their last as the company makes the shift to online only.
c79-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: How can readers support the survival of journalism, and what impact does their attention and spending have on the industry? Answer according to: With revenues dropping, Newsweek announced recently that their Dec. 31 print issue would be their last as the company makes the shift to online only. The Globe and Mail also recently put their content behind a paywall (again) — a ploy that the New York Times and others have tried and failed to capitalize on. Sun Media laid off 500 more employees. At times like this I wonder why I didn't go into underwater welding or some other field where there's long-term job security. Some will argue that what journalists — and especially print reporters — do is necessary for democracy, but the reality is that the majority of us work for private, for-profit publications that stand or fall on their own. It has to be this way, as it's the only way to stay independent from government spin and corporate influence. Unlike the CBC, BBC, PBS and a handful of other outlets, not many of us have any guaranteed funding. Newspapers are struggling to stay above water in this digital shift that is destroying, or has destroyed, so many once viable industries: music stores, movie rental stores, book stores, movie theatres, and more. We are the whip and buggy makers of our time watching the first cars drive by, and the free market will ultimately decide what lives and dies by how you divert your attention and spend money. When newspapers are closing offices and laying off staff, and institutions like Newsweek are abandoning a medium they helped to create, you know times are tough. And there's not much anyone can do about it. You could turn off Google News and the Huffington Post, stop using Craiglist and Kijiji, subscribe to paper papers and online media like The Globe and Mail, stop fast forwarding through the commercials on the shows you've PVRed and click on the odd online ad on websites that generate content. And if you go to a website that's republishing a story from somewhere, then you should click on the link to the original — those links add up and create more online advertising revenues for the actual producers of the content. And to everyone who still picks up Pique and other print papers, thank-you — you make all of this possible. But while these ideas are nice, they're not very realistic in the long term. Who knows? Maybe journalism will survive, and reporters like myself will continue to get paid for what we do. In the meantime, good luck Newsweek, the Globe and NYT — we're rooting for you.
Assistant: Readers can support the survival of journalism by diverting their attention and spending money towards the media outlets they want to see survive. This includes subscribing to paper and online media, clicking on online ads, and avoiding content aggregators that republish news without adding value to the original creators. However, the reality is that the media industry is facing tough times, and it's up to the free market to decide who survives and who doesn't. Ultimately, the fate of journalism depends on the willingness of readers to pay for quality content and the ability of media companies to adapt to the digital age.
User: Can you suggest some specific media outlets that I can support to help keep journalism alive?
Assistant: Sure, here are a few media outlets that you could consider supporting:

1. The New York Times - This newspaper has made significant investments in digital journalism, and they offer a variety of subscription options.

2. The Guardian - This UK-based newspaper is known for its investigative journalism and commitment to independent reporting.

3. ProPublica - This non-profit organization produces investigative journalism focused on holding the powerful accountable.

4. NPR - This public radio network provides in-depth reporting on a wide range of topics, and it relies on listener donations to continue its work.

5. The Intercept - This online news outlet was co-founded by journalist Glenn Greenwald and focuses on national security reporting and whistleblowers.

6. The Washington Post - This newspaper has made significant investments in digital journalism and has won numerous awards for its investigative reporting.

Remember, no matter which media outlets you choose to support, your attention and spending have an impact on the industry as a whole.
User: In the 1940s, there was broadcast TV, and advertisers paid the freight. Local stations beamed network and local programming to rabbit-ear antennas, and viewers watched live, free, ad-supported TV for a generation. It was in black and white, we had to watch it live, we couldn’t skip the commercials, and the whole country loved it.
Then came local cable and satellite delivery, which found wide adoption in the 1980s, and viewers who wanted their MTV, ESPN, Food Network, etc., paid part of the freight on a subscription basis, or what the normals call “the cable bill.” There were still ads, but you could get movies and some originals ad-free on HBO or Showtime if you wanted to pay extra.
From the 1990s to now, a steady evolution from programmable VCRs to mobile devices and smart TVs (heck, smart refrigerators!) and from standard-def cable to 4K streaming have made it easy to watch almost anything you want, on demand, on almost any device, for cheap, and without commercial interruptions. Pay TV service—which has shed millions of U.S. Subscribers over the last few years—costs $107 a month and is full of ads, but HD-quality, commercial-free Netflix costs $13 a month and has more quality programming than any mortal has time to watch.
So why is TV advertising on the verge of a huge 2019 with Viacom buying ad-supported Pluto TV, Hulu dropping the price of its ad-supported tier, Amazon launching ad-supported IMDB Freedive, Comcast announcing plans for an ad-supported NBCUniversal streaming service similar to the U.K.-based NowTV service that Comcast now owns, and WarnerMedia expected to launch an ad-supported service before the end of the year?
Free, ad-supported YouTube has 1.8 billion worldwide monthly active users.
On the Roku TV in my living room, I can watch Paul Thomas Anderson’s “The Master” and the first four seasons of “Dawson’s Creek” on the free, ad-supported Roku Channel.
On the Amazon Fire TV in the next room, I can watch Tom Cruise’s “The Last Samurai” and all seven seasons of “Without a Trace” on the free, ad-supported IMDB Freedive app.
On either TV, I can watch “Rob Riggle’s Ski Master Academy” on Sony Crackle, Martin Scorsese’s “Hugo” on TubiTV, dozens of live channels on Pluto TV and Xumo, and a live feed of ABC News Live or CBSN, all free and ad-supported.
Viewers are watching and distributors are continuing to put more and more money into AVOD, and that’s just the free stuff. You can watch most of the next-day episodes of ABC, NBC and Fox’s shows ad-supported for $6 a month on Hulu—which once had a free, ad-supported service—and CBS shows plus “Star Trek: Discovery” and other originals on CBS All Access ad-supported for $6 a month. You can also pay $4 a month more on either of those services to opt out of ads, but executives from both services have said that more subscribers choose the cheaper, ad-supported options.
So, why? In a world with 150 million Netflix subscribers watching an avalanche of great, new, ad-free programming, why is there a market for early 2000s TV reruns on free streaming apps?
The best answer, for now at least, is that there’s a big, diversified audience for all kinds of TV—from ad-supported reruns to $13-a-month Netflix—that’s getting more accustomed to watching what it wants and when it wants at little or no cost and getting less willing to pay $107 a month for it. As Greenfield often ends his Twitter posts, #GoodLuckBundle. How do free, ad-supported streaming apps like Roku Channel, IMDB Freedive, and Pluto TV compete with subscription services like Netflix and Hulu, and why do many viewers opt for ad-supported options?
Assistant: Free, ad-supported streaming apps like Roku Channel, IMDB Freedive and Pluto TV are competing with subscription services like Netflix and Hulu by offering a diversified audience a range of programming to watch at little or no cost. In a world where viewers are becoming more accustomed to watching TV when and where they want, and for a lower cost than traditional pay TV services, ad-supported options are becoming increasingly popular. Additionally, many subscribers are opting for the cheaper, ad-supported options on services like Hulu and CBS All Access, indicating that there is still a market for TV with ads, especially if it means paying less for their monthly subscription. Overall, the market for AVOD (advertising-supported video on demand) is growing as viewers seek out a variety of programming options at a lower cost, and advertisers are taking notice.
User: Can you give me some examples of the type of programming available on these free, ad-supported streaming apps?
Assistant: Sure, here are some examples of the type of programming available on free, ad-supported streaming apps:

- Roku Channel: classic TV shows (e.g. "I Love Lucy," "The Beverly Hillbillies"), recent movies (e.g. "The Matrix Revolutions," "Ender's Game"), and some original series (e.g. "Eye Candy," "The Demons of Dorian Gunn").

- IMDB Freedive: movies (e.g. "The Last Samurai," "Drive"), TV shows (e.g. "Heroes," "The Bachelor"), and some original content (e.g. "The IMDb Show," "No Small Parts").

- Pluto TV: live channels (e.g. News, sports, entertainment), classic TV shows (e.g. "Doctor Who," "The Twilight Zone"), and some original content (e.g. "Pluto TV Movies," "Onion News Network").

- Tubi TV: movies (e.g. "The Pursuit of Happyness," "Schindler's List"), TV shows (e.g. "The Office," "MasterChef"), and some original content (e.g. "Tubi Talks," "Listed").

- Sony Crackle: movies (e.g. "The Karate Kid," "S.W.A.T."), TV shows (e.g. "The Oath," "StartUp"), and some original content (e.g. "SuperMansion," "Rob Riggle's Ski Master Academy").

These are just a few examples, as there are many different free, ad-supported streaming apps out there, each with their own unique selection of programming.

Assistant: WarnerMedia's ad-supported streaming service is expected to launch in late 2019, but an exact date has not been announced. It is anticipated that the service will offer a mix of library content from Warner Bros. And Turner, as well as some original programming. The service will reportedly have a different pricing structure than other WarnerMedia offerings, like HBO, with a lower monthly subscription fee and ads in its programming. The company has not yet provided specific details about the programming that will be available on the service, but it is likely to include content from popular networks like HBO, TNT, TBS, and Cartoon Network.

Assistant: Sure, here are a few more ad-supported streaming apps that you might want to check out:

- Vudu: This app is owned by Walmart and offers a mix of free, ad-supported content (movies and TV shows) as well as paid rental and purchase options. It has a broad selection of movies and TV shows, including some recent releases.

- Crave: This Canadian streaming service offers ad-supported and subscription options (including a "Premium" tier that includes HBO content). Its free, ad-supported content includes TV shows, movies, and documentaries. 

- Xumo: This app offers a mix of live TV channels and on-demand content, including news, sports, and entertainment programming. Its live TV channels include both traditional networks (like ABC News and NBC) and digital-first channels (like Cheddar and Newsy).

- The CW: This app from The CW network offers free, ad-supported episodes of its popular shows (like "Riverdale," "The Flash," and "Supernatural"). You can watch the latest episodes a day after they air on TV.

- Shout! Factory TV: This app offers a mix of cult classic TV shows and movies, including some hard-to-find rarities. It also has some original content (like "MST3K," a revival of the cult-favorite TV show "Mystery Science Theater 3000").

User: How can readers support the survival of journalism, and what impact does their attention and spending have on the industry? Answer according to: With revenues dropping, Newsweek announced recently that their Dec. 31 print issue would be their last as the company makes the shift to online only. The Globe and Mail also recently put their content behind a paywall (again) — a ploy that the New York Times and others have tried and failed to capitalize on. Sun Media laid off 500 more employees. At times like this I wonder why I didn't go into underwater welding or some other field where there's long-term job security. Some will argue that what journalists — and especially print reporters — do is necessary for democracy, but the reality is that the majority of us work for private, for-profit publications that stand or fall on their own. It has to be this way, as it's the only way to stay independent from government spin and corporate influence. Unlike the CBC, BBC, PBS and a handful of other outlets, not many of us have any guaranteed funding. Newspapers are struggling to stay above water in this digital shift that is destroying, or has destroyed, so many once viable industries: music stores, movie rental stores, book stores, movie theatres, and more. We are the whip and buggy makers of our time watching the first cars drive by, and the free market will ultimately decide what lives and dies by how you divert your attention and spend money. When newspapers are closing offices and laying off staff, and institutions like Newsweek are abandoning a medium they helped to create, you know times are tough. And there's not much anyone can do about it. You could turn off Google News and the Huffington Post, stop using Craiglist and Kijiji, subscribe to paper papers and online media like The Globe and Mail, stop fast forwarding through the commercials on the shows you've PVRed and click on the odd online ad on websites that generate content. And if you go to a website that's republishing a story from somewhere, then you should click on the link to the original — those links add up and create more online advertising revenues for the actual producers of the content. And to everyone who still picks up Pique and other print papers, thank-you — you make all of this possible. But while these ideas are nice, they're not very realistic in the long term. Who knows? Maybe journalism will survive, and reporters like myself will continue to get paid for what we do. In the meantime, good luck Newsweek, the Globe and NYT — we're rooting for you.

Ultimately, the fate of journalism depends on the willingness of readers to pay for quality content and the ability of media companies to adapt to the digital age.

User: How can readers support the survival of journalism, and what impact does their attention and spending have on the industry? Answer according to: With revenues dropping, Newsweek announced recently that their Dec. 31 print issue would be their last as the company makes the shift to online only. At times like this I wonder why I didn't go into underwater welding or some other field where there's long-term job security. Some will argue that what journalists — and especially print reporters — do is necessary for democracy, but the reality is that the majority of us work for private, for-profit publications that stand or fall on their own. It has to be this way, as it's the only way to stay independent from government spin and corporate influence. Unlike the CBC, BBC, PBS and a handful of other outlets, not many of us have any guaranteed funding. Newspapers are struggling to stay above water in this digital shift that is destroying, or has destroyed, so many once viable industries: music stores, movie rental stores, book stores, movie theatres, and more. We are the whip and buggy makers of our time watching the first cars drive by, and the free market will ultimately decide what lives and dies by how you divert your attention and spend money. Yes, the quote is out of context, but I think Williams would forgive me since he was also concerned with world events and catastrophe. I believe that writers especially need the news because, for one, we deal with language and ideas. Second, the world outside expands the inner life of the writer. What do I read and what do I find? I am a very slow reader, and on Sundays, faced with umpteen sections of the New York Times, I try to get through the Week in Review and, later over lunch, the first section and something from the Book Review. (If I’m feeling frisky, I’ll look at real estate classifieds for “fun” or a Guy Trebay piece on fashion.) During the week I read over whatever jumps out at me—especially in Tuesday’s Science section. I also pick up the Daily News for the comics and horoscope and a different take on events. Plus I relish its fuggedaboudit-tone. And on Fridays I pick up the Wall Street Journal, fancying that it might offer an alternate view; at the very least, I like to check out their Weekend section.
I am not suggesting that a writer has to write about the news. Of course no one has to write social or political poems. (Although I do encourage my students to write a piece using “outside material”—just as I encourage them to write a tanka or a sonnet.) My interest is in language and ideas. And I have always found inspiration in newspapers. Also, I know I would not be the poet—or the person—I have become without the news in its many forms, including television news that ranges from PBS to Comedy Central.

The material itself triggers deep emotional material in much the way a smell evokes a childhood memory. I certainly would not wish to dismiss or disregard this kind of rich dimension. (Apparently, even Emily Dickinson kept up with the news—especially sensational crimes and disasters.) On the other hand, I admit that reading the news, on paper or online, will not necessarily produce more radiant poetry. Still, it will make one’s life richer—and that is a step in a potentially radiant direction. And it will make each person more of a citizen of this fragile planet.

User: How does the proposed ordinance shift power away from employers when it comes to paying and scheduling their employees?
Generate according to: Steven Mitchell Sack, “The Employee’s Lawyer,” will appear on “Fox & Friends” on Saturday, February 27 at 6:45 a.m. To discuss the new rules that are being proposed in Seattle on how companies establish their employees’ work schedules.
The Seattle City Council recently proposed a set of rules that shifts the power away from employers when it comes to how employees are not only paid but scheduled to work. Although it is still being drafted, the proposed ordinance would guarantee workers at least eleven hours of downtime between shifts, allow workers to receive their work schedule two weeks in advance or else be paid time-and-a-half if shifts are added inside that timeframe and require employers to pay employees for a few hours of work not performed if shifts are taken away.
This 11-hour downtime provision in the bill is to prevent the practice of “clopenings,” in which employees who stay late at night to close are also asked to open up the store the next day. The city also ratified raising the minimum wage to $15 an hour.
Fox News Channel can be seen on Channel 26 (cablevision). Channel 360(DirecTV), Channel 205 (DISH Network), Channel 315 (RCN Cable). Channel 44/202 (Time Warner), and Channel 118/1543 (FiOS).
Assistant: The proposed ordinance in Seattle would shift power away from employers by placing restrictions on how employees are paid and scheduled to work. Employers would be required to guarantee their employees at least eleven hours of downtime between shifts, pay time-and-a-half for last-minute schedule changes, and compensate their employees for lost time if shifts are taken away. These new rules would give employees more control over their work schedules and ensure that they are fairly compensated for their time. This would reduce the ability of employers to exploit their workers by forcing them to work long hours without adequate breaks or compensation. In essence, the proposed ordinance would level the playing field between employers and employees in Seattle.

These provisions are intended to provide workers with greater stability and predictability regarding their work schedules and compensation.

c103-m1.summary: The Duke of Edinburgh Award program is designed for all young people to participate in and benefit from, regardless of their career aspirations or goals.
c103-m1.source_conv_dialogue:
User: Can you please paraphrase the benefits of having a marketing mentor for your marketing manager? Answer according to: Get the best out of your marketing manager.
You have a marketing manager who is good at doing marketing activities, however there is a marketing strategy gap and you lack the time or the expertise to direct, guide and mentor.
As your marketing mentor, we’ll work directly with your marketing manager, developing the marketing strategy together and sharing our extensive marketing leadership expertise. Your marketing manager will become focused, motivated and results-driven, and will learn valuable strategic marketing skills along the way.
By understanding the dynamics behind marketing, taking a strategic approach, and therefore making educated choices instead of trial and error, your marketing success will become consistent and more certain.
We’ve helped many marketing managers transform into highly effective marketing directors, who are loyal and are focused on creating real business value.
Assistant: The advantages of having a marketing mentor for your marketing manager, with the goal of getting the best out of them, are numerous. Firstly, it can help bridge any gaps in marketing strategy, which can be difficult to manage if you lack the time or expertise to do so. By working directly with your marketing manager, a marketing mentor can share their extensive experience in marketing leadership to develop the strategy collectively. Your marketing manager will become more focused, motivated and results-driven, and will learn valuable strategic marketing skills in the process. By using a strategic approach to marketing and making informed choices, your success in marketing will become more consistent and reliable. Furthermore, many marketing managers who have worked with a mentor have transformed into highly effective marketing directors, who are loyal and focused on generating genuine business value.
User: Can you please provide more information on how the marketing mentorship program has benefited other marketing managers in the past?
Assistant: I do not have access to specific information about individual cases of the marketing mentorship program. However, based on past experiences and general knowledge, there are several ways in which a marketing mentorship program can benefit a marketing manager. 

firstly, it can help to develop their strategic thinking skills, which are essential for successful marketing. By working alongside an experienced marketing mentor, the manager can learn to analyze market trends, identify opportunities and challenges, and develop effective marketing strategies.

secondly, the mentorship program can help the marketing manager improve their communication and leadership skills. A good marketing mentor will encourage the manager to engage with their team, build strong relationships with stakeholders, and communicate effectively to both internal and external audiences.

thirdly, the mentorship program can help the marketing manager stay up-to-date with the latest marketing trends and best practices. This can be especially important in fast-moving industries, where marketing approaches can quickly become outdated.

finally, by providing ongoing support and feedback, the mentorship program can help the marketing manager to continuously improve their performance and achieve their goals. Overall, the mentorship program can be a valuable investment in the development of a marketing manager, and can lead to significant benefits for the organization as a whole.
User: Can you provide specific examples of notable young individuals who have completed the Duke of Edinburgh Award program and gone on to achieve success in their careers or personal lives?
Assistant: Yes, here are some examples of young individuals who have completed the Duke of Edinburgh Award program and have gone on to achieve success in their careers or personal lives:

1. Prince Edward, Earl of Wessex: Prince Edward completed his Gold Award in 1986 and has been a patron of the Duke of Edinburgh's Award since 2015. He is also the chairman of the International Council of the Duke of Edinburgh's International Award Association.

2. Nicola Adams: Nicola Adams, a two-time Olympic boxing champion, completed her Bronze and Silver Duke of Edinburgh's awards. She has gone on to become an ambassador for the program and has helped to promote it to young people across the UK.

3. Bear Grylls: Bear Grylls completed his Gold Award in 1984 and has since become a renowned adventurer, author, and television personality. He is also a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society and has been presented with several awards for his contributions to outdoor activities.

4. Ellie Simmonds: Ellie Simmonds, a Paralympic swimmer, completed her Gold Award in 2011. She has won 14 Paralympic medals and has been appointed as a Member of the Order of the British Empire for her services to swimming.

5. Emma Watson: Emma Watson, an actress and activist, completed her Bronze Duke of Edinburgh's award. She has since become a UN Women Goodwill Ambassador, a prominent advocate for women's rights, and an influential voice for social justice causes.

6. Tim Peake: Tim Peake, a British astronaut, completed his Gold Duke of Edinburgh's award in 1990. He became the first British astronaut to visit the International Space Station in 2015 and has since become a prominent advocate for science education and exploration.

These individuals are just a few examples of the many young people who have completed the Duke of Edinburgh's Award program and have gone on to achieve success in their careers and personal lives. The program has helped to instil self-confidence, resilience, and a commitment to excellence in countless young people across the UK and around the world.
User: Wow, these are some really impressive individuals. It seems like the Duke of Edinburgh Award program really sets people up for success. Do you think it's worth doing even if you don't necessarily want to achieve fame or recognition?
Assistant: Yes, absolutely! While the program's alumni include some well-known and accomplished figures, the Duke of Edinburgh Award program is designed for all young people to participate in and benefit from, regardless of their career aspirations or goals.

The program is focused on personal development and encourages participants to challenge themselves, build life skills, and gain practical experience in areas like leadership, teamwork, and community service. These are all valuable qualities and experiences that can benefit individuals in every aspect of their lives, whether they go on to achieve fame and recognition or not.

By completing the Duke of Edinburgh Award program, young people can gain the self-confidence, resilience, and sense of responsibility that come with achieving personal goals and contributing to their communities. And in doing so, they can develop the skills and attributes that will help them succeed in whatever they choose to do, make a positive impact in the world, and lead fulfilling lives.
User: It's great to hear that the Duke of Edinburgh Award program is focused on personal development and building life skills. How long does it usually take to complete the program? Is it something that can be done while studying or working?
Assistant: The time it takes to complete the Duke of Edinburgh Award program varies depending on the level of the award that you are aiming for and the amount of time you have available to commit to the program. In general:

- Bronze level: typically takes around 6-12 months to complete, and requires a minimum of 6 months of participation in an activity, 3 months of physical activity, 3 months of skill development, and 3 months of volunteering.

User: What impact have recent policy interventions had on the use of the K-P index as an economic indicator? Answer according to: Last year's release of the ‘Kavanagh-Putland index’ showed that the ratio of property sales to GDP was slightly higher in 2012-13 than in 2011-12. The RBA lowered the cash rate by 25 points in May 2013 and again in August 2013. Since then, lending for acquisitions of owner-occupied homes and investment homes, especially the latter, has continued to rise in proportion to GDP. The investment frenzy has been led by New South Wales, where the investors' share of finance commitments (excluding refinancing) has smashed through the record set in 2003-4, yielding an unexpected stamp-duty bonanza for the state government.
Curiously, NSW also led the charge in terminating first home owners' grants for established homes. Unfortunately the Commonwealth made no matching reforms to negative gearing, with the result that first home buyers (FHBs) found it even harder to compete with investors in the market for established homes — unless, of course, they decided to make their first home an investment home, using negative gearing to service larger mortgages than they could carry as owner-occupants.
As previously noted, the year-on-year change in the K-P index was a reasonably good predictor of Australian recessions prior to the massive policy interventions of 2008-9 (a fall of more than 18% signalled a recession). Since then, governments and central banks have paid closer attention to the housing market. Policy interventions designed to influence that market invalidate predictions about its internal dynamics, while interventions designed to counteract the influence of that market on the wider economy reduce its value as an economic indicator.
The critical question is how long the authorities can keep the music going. On interest rates, David Llewellyn-Smith has remarked: “The RBA is in the process of throwing away its ammunition and when the next crisis strikes the chamber will be empty.” His graph of investor mortgage commitments suggests the trend cannot continue for long, even under the most favourable conditions, before investors pull in their horns as in 2003-4. Under less favourable conditions, investors are more willing than owner-occupants to stop buying or rush for the exits. That makes the present market unusually vulnerable to the mining investment “cliff” or any external shock.
The K-P index is an estimate of the ratio of property sales to GDP. It is called an “index”, rather than a simple “ratio”, because it is based on a varying sample.
Only Victoria has sales figures dating back to 1972. Qld, WA and NT join the sample in 1979, Tasmania and the ACT in '84, SA in '85, and NSW in '89. Initially, Bryan Kavanagh obtained figures from government offices. But, as more and more governments monetized their data, more and more figures had to be obtained from secondary sources. There were cases in which the figure for a particular jurisdiction in a particular year was rejected as unreliable, e.g. Because it was an outlier or had been subject to an unusually large “correction”. More recently, using figures from RP Data, we plugged the gaps from 2001-2 onward.
To deal with missing or rejected sales figures, we add up the property sales in those jurisdictions for which reliable figures are available, and divide by the estimated sum of Gross State Products (GSPs) in the same jurisdictions, so that jurisdictions without reliable figures are simply excluded from the sample.
I say “estimated sum” because the GSP figures from the ABS are also incomplete; they go back only as far as 1984-5 and are released later than the corresponding GDP figures. Furthermore, due to an apparent change in methodology, GSPs do not add up to GDP before 1989-90. Accordingly, for each year in which GSPs are known, the GSP for each jurisdiction is divided by the total GSP to obtain the “GSP fraction”, which is then multiplied by GDP to obtain the “estimated GSP” for that jurisdiction. For earlier/later years, the earliest/latest available GSP fractions are used. The extrapolations of GSP fractions affect the index in those years for which the sales figures are incomplete. In the current release, the estimated GSPs for 2013-4 are based on the GSP fractions for 2012-13; but this does not affect the index because the sales figures are complete.
A further problem is that the figures from Victoria's Valuer-General were for the calendar year while annual figures for other jurisdictions were for the “financial year ended...” RP Data was able to supply quarterly figures for Victoria, but only from 1975 onward. Thus the first three data points on each graph are for calendar years, and the fourth is for the first half of calendar year 1975, and the rest are for financial years. We use seasonally adjusted GDP figures to ensure that the result for the single half-year is not affected by the seasonal variation in GDP, although it is still affected by any seasonal variation in sales.
We continue to use RP Data's figures for Victoria. In the above graphs, we also use RP Data's figures for 2011-12 onward in NSW, Qld, Tas, NT and ACT, for April 2013 onward in WA, for 2007-8 in NSW, and for 2009-10 in Tas. Excluded from the sample are NSW in 2000-1 (which fortunately is not a critical year for interpreting the graphs), NT in 1997-8 (for which the geographic coverage does not match other years), and ACT in 1991-2. Obviously the last two exclusions make little difference to the calculated index.
Assistant: Recent policy interventions, such as the RBA's lowering of the cash rate and government changes to first home owners' grants and negative gearing, have had an impact on the use of the K-P index as an economic indicator. These interventions have influenced the dynamics of the housing market and made it less reliable as an indicator of the wider economy. Additionally, the K-P index is based on a varying sample of property sales to GDP ratios, which makes it susceptible to missing or unreliable data. Overall, while the K-P index can provide some insight into the housing market, it should be used cautiously and in conjunction with other economic indicators.
User: Can you use the K-P index to predict a recession in the current economic climate?
Assistant: It is difficult to use the K-P index to predict a recession in the current economic climate due to recent policy interventions and the fact that the index is based on a varying sample. Additionally, the housing market has become less reliable as an economic indicator due to these interventions. While changes in the K-P index can still provide some insight into the housing market and wider economy, caution should be exercised when using it to make predictions. Other economic indicators, such as GDP growth, inflation, and employment rates, should also be considered in predicting a recession.
User: Can you provide any insights on the potential impact of the mining investment "cliff" on the housing market and the wider economy?
Assistant: The mining investment "cliff" refers to the sharp decline in mining investment that occurred after the peak in 2012-2013. This decline has had significant impacts on the Australian economy, including slower economic growth and a higher unemployment rate, particularly in the mining-dependent regions.

In terms of the housing market, the "cliff" has resulted in a decrease in demand for housing in mining-dependent regions, where housing prices have fallen significantly. This has led to a ripple effect in other regions as well, as investors have shifted their focus away from the mining sector and towards other investment opportunities.

However, there have been some positive impacts on the housing market, as lower interest rates have made it easier for households to obtain mortgages and invest in real estate. This has led to increased demand for housing in some areas, particularly in Sydney and Melbourne.

Overall, the impact of the mining investment "cliff" on the housing market and wider economy is complex and varied. While it has resulted in significant challenges, such as declining property prices and rising unemployment, it has also opened up new opportunities for the housing market and contributed to lower interest rates, which have benefited many households.

That may be the case for a small majority of youth, but for most, they were forced out of their homes or left because the abuse they were facing was too much for them to bear.
